opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the core idea is something we called *selectivity*.

For a few years before Mamba, my collaborators and I had been working on structured state space models like S4. These are basically recurrent models with a fixed-size hidden state that gets updated over time. They had some really nice properties: they scale linearly in sequence length, they handle very long-range dependencies well, and they can be computed efficiently as either a convolution or a recurrence. They did great on things like audio and other continuous signals, but they consistently lagged behind Transformers on discrete, information-dense data like language.

When we dug into why, the problem was that those models were *linear time-invariant*. The dynamics, meaning how the state evolves and what gets written into or read out of it, were the same at every time step regardless of the input. So the model couldn't decide, based on content, "this token matters, remember it," or "this is filler, ignore it," or "reset my state here." Attention gets that kind of content-based routing almost for free, because it can always look back at everything.

So the central change in Mamba was to make the key parameters of the state space model functions of the input. The step size and the input and output projections vary with each token. That lets the model selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence, which turns out to be essential for language-like tasks. Conceptually, it connects back to gating in classical RNNs like LSTMs, but within the more principled SSM framework.

The catch is that once you make the model input-dependent, you lose the convolution trick that made S4 efficient. So the other half of the breakthrough was really an engineering one: a hardware-aware parallel scan algorithm. We keep the expanded state in fast on-chip SRAM rather than materializing it in GPU memory, fuse the operations, and recompute intermediate values in the backward pass. That made the selective recurrence actually fast in practice.

Put those together and you get a model that's linear in sequence length, has constant-time inference per token with no growing KV cache, and for the first time with this family of models, matches or comes close to Transformers on language modeling at the scales we tested. To me, the deeper takeaway is about compression. A recurrent model has to compress its history into a fixed state, and selectivity is what lets it compress *intelligently* instead of treating everything equally.

r001.rationale: It calls selectivity the core idea and describes the hardware-aware parallel scan as making the selective recurrence fast in practice.

r002.rationale: It connects selectivity to LSTM-style gating and explains that the model can selectively retain or forget information based on each token.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Mamba’s input-dependent state-space parameters with earlier models whose dynamics were the same at every time step regardless of input.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the central thing is selection, which sounds small but it changes what a state space model can do.

For context, the earlier structured state space models, S4 and its relatives, were essentially linear time-invariant systems. The dynamics were fixed. The same transition matrix, the same input and output projections, applied at every position in the sequence. That gave you some wonderful properties. You could compute the whole thing as a convolution, train it in parallel, and run it as a recurrence at inference with constant memory. They did very well on long-range benchmarks and on continuous signals like audio. But they were mediocre at language, and for a long time people assumed that was a capacity issue or a scaling issue.

The realization was that the problem was more fundamental. A time-invariant system cannot look at a token and decide whether to remember it or ignore it. It treats every input the same way. Attention, by contrast, is content-aware by construction. It gets to choose what to attend to based on what the data actually is. Language is full of that kind of thing, where you need to carry one piece of information for a long time and discard most of what comes in between.

So the move in Mamba was to let the SSM parameters depend on the input. The step size, the input projection, the output projection all become functions of the current token. Now the model can effectively open or close the gate on its hidden state, reset it, or hold onto something indefinitely, depending on content. Conceptually it's quite close to the gating in an LSTM or GRU, and the paper spells out that connection. But it's done in a way that keeps the state large and structured rather than a small dense vector.

The catch is that once the parameters vary with the input, you lose the convolutional view. You can no longer precompute a kernel and do an FFT. That's where the second half of the contribution comes in, which is really a systems idea. We realized that you can still compute the recurrence efficiently as a parallel scan, and if you're careful about where the state lives in GPU memory, materializing it only in fast SRAM and never writing the full expanded state out to high-bandwidth memory, you get something that's actually faster than attention in wall-clock terms and scales linearly in sequence length. Without that hardware-aware implementation, selectivity would have been a nice idea that nobody could afford to train.

The other piece was just simplifying the architecture. Instead of interleaving an SSM layer with an MLP block the way most of the earlier models did, we folded everything into one homogeneous block. That made it cleaner and, it turned out, didn't cost anything.

So if I had to name a single breakthrough, it's that recognition that selectivity, the ability to compress context in a content-dependent way, is the thing that separates models that work on language from models that don't. And then doing the engineering needed to make a selective recurrent model actually competitive on real hardware. Those two things together are what let an attention-free model match transformers at the scales we tested.

r001.rationale: It identifies input-dependent selectivity as central and explains how a parallel scan and GPU memory design make the recurrence efficient.

r002.rationale: It says the model can open or close a gate on its hidden state based on the current token, deciding what to retain or discard.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Mamba’s input-dependent parameters with earlier state-space models’ fixed dynamics and shared projections at every sequence position.

astra-6.text:
I think the central breakthrough is making state space models selective—letting the model decide, based on the input, what information to retain and what to forget.

With a traditional state space model, the dynamics are fixed across the sequence. That gives you some very useful computational properties, but it makes tasks like selectively remembering a particular token difficult. With Mamba, those dynamics can depend on the current input, so the model can filter information as it processes the sequence.

The other crucial piece is making that efficient. Introducing input dependence means you lose the convolutional computation that earlier models relied on. So we developed a hardware-aware scan algorithm that lets you train efficiently on GPUs while preserving linear scaling with sequence length. It’s really the combination of content-dependent selection and an efficient implementation that makes the approach work.

r001.rationale: It identifies input-dependent selection and the hardware-aware scan as the combination that makes Mamba efficient.

r002.rationale: It says Mamba filters information based on the current input, but does not connect selectivity to gating that controls how much attention incoming inputs receive.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Mamba’s input-dependent dynamics with traditional state-space models’ fixed dynamics across the sequence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central breakthrough is making state space models selective—letting the model decide, based on the input, what information to retain and what to forget. Earlier models had very efficient computation, but their dynamics were fixed. That makes it difficult to do things like remember a particular piece of information while ignoring everything in between.

With Mamba, those dynamics depend on the content. The challenge is that you lose some of the computational shortcuts that made earlier state space models efficient, so the other key piece is a hardware-aware algorithm that makes that selective recurrence run efficiently on GPUs.

Those two ideas together give you content-dependent reasoning over a sequence while keeping computation linear in sequence length and a fixed-size state during generation.

r001.rationale: It identifies input-dependent selectivity and a hardware-aware GPU algorithm that makes the selective recurrence efficient.

r002.rationale: It describes retaining or forgetting information based on input, but does not connect selectivity to gating that controls how much attention is given to incoming inputs.

r003.rationale: It explicitly contrasts Mamba’s content-dependent dynamics with earlier state-space models’ fixed dynamics.
